Crude oil remains under pressure as demand concerns continue to weigh despite high US-Iran tensions
body: Crude oil has been under selling pressure despite no changes on the geopolitical front. Growth concerns and global stock market rout have been the likely culprit for the weakness as lower future demand expectations naturally push prices lower despite continued supply constraints.

On the Middle East front, Trump said that he favours resuming military action against Iran after the new year if no agreement is reached, while indicating that indirect negotiations remain ongoing but have made no concrete progress.

Meanwhile, Israeli sources reported that Netanyahu is considering striking Iran without US approval, although military intelligence warned that such a move could trigger a multi-front conflict. Israel is also reportedly preparing for a scenario in which the US launches initial strikes without Israeli involvement, with Israeli officials increasingly convinced that a US attack has already been decided and that only the timing remains uncertain.

Overall, there’s been no de-escalation nor improvement in the US-Iran situation as the risk of another direct military confrontation remains high. Oil prices might remain under pressure but we will likely need a bigger selloff in the stock market, an even more hawkish Fed or weak economic data to keep the bearish momentum going.

On the daily chart, we can see that crude oil (CFD contract) is approaching the key 80.00 handle. If the price gets there, we can expect the buyers to step in, with a defined risk below the level, to position for a rally into the 110.00 level. The sellers, on the other hand, will look for a break to increase the bearish bets into the 68.00 support next.

On the 4 hour chart, we have a downward trendline defining the bearish structure. If we get a pullback, we can expect the sellers to lean on the trendline, with a defined risk above it, to position for a drop into new lows. The buyers, on the other hand, will want to see the price breaking higher to pile in for a rally into the 110.00 level next, with the 92.50 level as the first target.

On the 1 hour chart, we have a minor resistance zone around the 84.00 handle. The sellers will likely continue to step in around the resistance, with a defined risk above it, to keep pushing into new lows. The buyers, on the other hand, will look for a break higher to extend the pullback into the trendline next. The red lines define the average daily range for today.
Today we have the US Flash PMIs. Tomorrow, we get the US Consumer Confidence report. On Wednesday, we have the US Core PCE price index and the latest US Jobless Claims figures.

news.title: Gold trims losses amid broad short-covering across markets as growth concerns linger. What's next?
body: Gold extended the losses on Friday but eventually bounced around the key 3,500 level likely due to some short-covering after the aggressive selloff. The precious metal then extended the gains in the APAC session amid a broad-based recovery in many other markets.

The capitulation in the final part of last week seemed to be driven by another liquidation wave caused by the stock market rout. In fact, the US dollar remained relatively flat, real yields fell, and rate hike expectations actually eased following equity losses.

As mentioned on Friday, the hawkish repricing is now over, and we might even see a dovish repricing in the next months if the equity losses extend further and economic data deteriorates. Therefore, the risk-reward for more downside has weakened, although we haven’t got any bullish catalyst yet to position for a sustained reversal.

Today, we get the Flash US PMIs. The data might provide the first bullish catalyst if it surprises to the downside as growth concerns may increase further and rate hike bets further down the curve should be unwound. Strong data, on the other hand, could add some more downward pressure in the short-term.
Looking ahead, gold will likely need support from a dovish repricing in interest rate expectations either from weaker data, dovish Fed commentary or an end to the Iran war.

On the daily chart, we can see that gold (CFD contract) rejected the key 3,500 level as the buyers stepped in to position for a correction into the major downward trendline. If the price rolls over and breaks below the level, we can expect the sellers to increase the bearish bets and target the 3,100 level next.

On the 4 hour chart, we have a downward trendline defining the bearish momentum. If we get a pullback, we can expect the sellers to lean on the trendline, with a defined risk above it, to keep targeting new lows. The buyers, on the other hand, will want to see the price breaking higher to increase the bullish bets into the major downward trendline next.

On the 1 hour chart, we can see the price broke above the minor downward trendline that was defining the bearish momentum on this timeframe. This generally signals a loss of momentum. If the price pulls back to retest the broken trendline around the 3,570 level, we can expect the buyers to step in there, with a defined risk below the broken trendline, to keep pushing into new highs. The sellers, on the other hand, will look for a break to pile in for a drop back into the 3,500 level, targeting a break below it. The red lines define the average daily range for today.
Today we have the US Flash PMIs. Tomorrow, we get the US Consumer Confidence report. On Wednesday, we have the US Core PCE price index and the latest US Jobless Claims figures.

news.title: Peterson: The Fed's chairman sees an AI revolution coming. Now he has to figure out what it means
body: Artificial intelligence is about to sweep through the economy. The Federal Reserve is bracing for impact.

"We are at a hinge point in the U.S. economy," Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said at a conference he convened in San Francisco on Monday. But exactly when and how the economy could turn, and what that means for interest rates and inflation, isn't yet clear.

The meeting of Warsh's AI task force saw the new Fed chairman publicly asking the questions Americans will ultimately expect him to answer. He hinted at a few of his private views on whether white-collar workers could soon face massive job losses, but he largely left the speculation to an array of experts he has assembled to advise the Fed.

With the technology racing ahead, Warsh won't be able to put off giving his own answers much longer. AI lab Anthropic plans to price the shares for its initial public offering on Wednesday and could raise as much as $64 billion at a $1.4 trillion valuation. Vast spending from AI firms is prompting the Fed to contemplate raising interest rates in December to slow down the rate of price increases as the tech sector heats up the economy.

Meanwhile Americans are souring on some aspects of the technology. The Nov. 3 midterms saw voters enact an array of state-level measures to slow down construction of the data centers that are essential to powering AI.

Warsh moderated three out of four sessions at Monday's event and was involved in selecting the speakers. Among them was one of the few prominent Democrats who was willing to speak out against that anti-data center trend.

It is "a very troubling sign" that so many anti-data center measures passed in the midterms, Gina Raimondo said. She is a former secretary of Commerce under President Joe Biden and a former governor of Rhode Island.
Stopping AI "would be very bad for America" and for the people who voted for the measures, Raimondo said.
Warsh didn't say whether he shares that view, and how it would translate into monetary policy isn't exactly clear.

The event was an unusual one for the Fed. The central bank employs a small army of Ph.D. economists who can rapidly weigh in on anything affecting the U.S. and global economies. But in keeping with his long-standing critiques of the Fed as insular and outdated, Warsh has chosen to draw expertise from outside the institution to help it figure out how to think about what AI will do to productivity and jobs.
Warsh has assembled a task force on that issue, alongside four others devoted to aspects of Fed policymaking.

The public heard Monday from one of the three official members of the task force: venture capitalist Marc Andreessen. Warsh went to Stanford University with Andreessen's wife, and the two have been longtime friends. Another task force member, Stanford economist Chad Jones, is on leave and working at Anthropic and couldn't speak during the company's blackout period ahead of the IPO. The third, Xbox CEO Asha Sharma, didn't attend the event.

Andreessen is hugely optimistic about the promise of AI as a technology, but believes the government won't let Americans experience its full effects. Heavy regulation in areas such as healthcare and education mean technology can't replace people's jobs in those sectors, he said.

"To the extent our economy is a free market economy, then maybe you could see the, let's say, extremely rapid displacement scenarios people are talking about," Andreessen said. "But we've mostly outlawed the kind of job transition that … both the utopians the doomers talk about."

news.title: Japan core inflation soars to highest this year as energy subsidy expiry pushes up consumer prices
body: Core inflation in Japan soared to a fresh high in 2026, coming in at 2.2% in October as higher energy costs and their knock-on effects pushed up prices in the wider economy.
Core inflation, which strips out prices of food, was lower than the 2.3% expected by Reuters-polled economists, but was higher than the 2.1% in prior month.

Headline inflation came in at 2.3% compared with September's 2.1%, while the so-called "core-core" inflation, which strips out prices of fresh food and energy, dipped slightly to 2.2% from 2.4% in the month before, government data released on Friday showed.

Energy subsidies for households expired in September, exposing consumers to higher prices brought about by the Iran war. Energy prices climbed 2.2% in October, a sharp spike from the 0.6% decline in September. Gas prices jumped 5.8% compared to the 2.4% rise the month before.
Fuel, light and water charges also saw a considerable acceleration, increasing 3.4% compared to last month's 0.8%.
Following the release, the Nikkei 225 index was down 2.1%, while the 10-year JGB yield fell 2 basis points to 2.805%.
Japan has reportedly approved reintroduction of energy subsidies in December to stave off higher imported energy prices as higher prices crimp growth, hitting consumption and net exports.

The October inflation reading is likely to push the Bank of Japan toward another rate hike in December, despite an unexpected contraction in economic growth in the third quarter. Data from LSEG indicates that there is a 72% chance of a 25 basis point hike from the Bank of Japan.

On Wednesday, BOJ Governor Kazuo Ueda told parliament that the central bank was also "mindful" of the weak yen and rising crude prices, saying that these could hurt ⁠households' real income and weigh on consumption more than expected.
The yen marginally strengthened to trade at 159.59 against the dollar after the data release.
Japan's inflation is likely to still stay above 2% for the rest of 2026 and into the first quarter of 2027, according to Ma Tieying, senior economist at DBS Group Research.
She pointed out that while higher energy prices and yen weakness have contributed to headline inflation, the recent upturn is also supported by domestic factors.

"Wage growth has remained above 3% for nine consecutive months, pointing to a broader pickup in underlying inflation as stronger wage gains feed through to services prices and household spending. This suggests a more durable wage–price cycle is taking hold."
Ma expects the BOJ to raise rates in its December meeting, then twice more in 2027, bringing its terminal rate to 2%.
